content: The guidelines emphasize the importance of person-centered HIV care and monitoring, particularly for pregnant and breastfeeding women, as well as their infants. Optimized second-line antiretroviral therapy (ART) regimens, which may be dolutegravir (DTG)-based or protease inhibitor (PI)-based, are recommended. Delayed transition to second-line regimens can result in increased morbidity and mortality. Specific data elements are recommended to monitor the transition to optimized regimens for children, including the percentage of children on DTG-based regimens, viral load (VL) testing at six months post-ART initiation, and annual testing thereafter. Other indicators include TB prophylaxis, co-trimoxazole prophylaxis coverage, multi-month ARV dispensing, VL suppression rates, psychosocial support, ART attrition, and the number of children on second-line ART. As children transition into adolescent and adult care, longitudinal monitoring with linked patient records is critical to ensure continuity of person-centered care. Strengthening the monitoring of the prevention of mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT) cascade is essential, focusing on outcomes such as viral suppression, early infant diagnosis, and tracking service milestones during the vertical transmission risk period. This includes monitoring the health of pregnant and breastfeeding women living with HIV and the risk of vertical transmission to their infants. The guidelines also highlight the importance of retesting pregnant women with unknown or HIV-negative status during late pregnancy, particularly in high-burden settings. Retesting at specific intervals (e.g., 14 weeks, six months, or nine months) is recommended for those at high ongoing risk. Indicators for monitoring vertical transmission have been updated to include early infant diagnosis (EID) coverage, infant ARV prophylaxis coverage, ART coverage in pregnant and breastfeeding women, and final PMTCT outcomes. These indicators are linked to critical time points in the vertical transmission risk period and aim to strengthen data collection, quality assurance, and use for patient care and program management. The guidelines stress the integration of PMTCT and pediatric HIV care with maternal, newborn, and child health (MNCH) services. Monitoring systems should track mother-infant pairs across service delivery points and ensure robust systems for assigning unique identifiers (UIDs) to link records. HIV information should be integrated into existing MNCH records or electronic health systems. This integration supports early PMTCT interventions, monitoring PMTCT cascade outcomes, and cross-referrals between HIV and MNCH services. The updated indicators focus on outcomes such as viral suppression and early infant diagnosis, alongside intermediate outcomes like ART coverage during pregnancy and breastfeeding and infant ARV prophylaxis. Seven national priority indicators have been designated to assist countries in focusing resources on strengthening data sources, collection tools, and quality assurance mechanisms. These updates are reflected in revised patient monitoring tools and minimum datasets for HIV care. For pregnant women living with HIV, it is crucial to ensure they are referred to appropriate MNCH/PMTCT services and that their HIV status is recorded in their patient card or electronic medical record (EMR). Women identified as living with HIV in MNCH settings should be enrolled in HIV care and entered into the ART register once started on ART. Monitoring tools should capture the full spectrum of care for HIV-exposed infants, including ARV and co-trimoxazole prophylaxis, timely HIV nucleic acid testing, appropriate infant feeding practices, and final outcome testing. If an infant is confirmed HIV-positive, a separate record and UID should be created for the child. The guidance also includes updates to data elements, such as VL testing during pregnancy and delivery, hepatitis B screening during antenatal care, and administration of the birth-dose hepatitis B vaccine. These updates aim to enhance the monitoring of maternal and child health outcomes and support the elimination of vertical transmission of HIV, syphilis, and hepatitis B.
